memberlounge.summary: A membership platform for people who run paid communities and were stitching one together out of a payment link, a spreadsheet, and a Discord invite bot.

problem.lead: Running a paid community is three jobs pretending to be one: take the money, decide who is still a member today, and get those people into the room. Every off-the-shelf answer solves one and leaves the other two as manual work.
points: Payment links have no idea what a membership is — a failed renewal is an email nobody reads, not a revoked seat.
Access lived in a spreadsheet that went stale the moment a card expired, so people paid for weeks after losing access and others kept access for months after cancelling.
Owners had no honest read on churn: Stripe knew about charges, the community tool knew about logins, and nothing joined the two.
Every organiser rebuilt the same brittle glue with webhooks and zaps, and it broke silently.

solution.lead: One service owns the membership lifecycle end to end. Billing state is the source of truth, entitlements are derived from it, and every surface — dashboard, invite flow, API — reads the same derived state.
points: Stripe webhooks land in an idempotent event log; entitlements are recomputed from that log rather than patched in place, so a replayed or out-of-order event can't corrupt access.
A single `hasAccess(member, feature)` check backs the UI, the API, and the invite bot — no second implementation to drift.
Dunning is a state machine, not a cron of emails: grace period, retry, downgrade, revoke, each step visible in the member's timeline.
Owner dashboard streams live over WebSockets — joins, renewals, cancellations, MRR — so the numbers match what Stripe says without an export step.

notes.title: Idempotency before features
notes.body: Stripe will deliver the same webhook twice and occasionally out of order. The first version applied deltas directly to a member row and drifted within a week. Storing raw events and deriving entitlements made the whole system replayable — a bug fix is a recompute, not a data migration.

notes.title: One authorization path
notes.body: The invite bot originally had its own idea of who was a member, which meant two code paths and two sets of bugs. Collapsing everything onto one entitlement check cost a refactor and removed an entire class of support ticket.

notes.title: Real-time without a second backend
notes.body: The dashboard needed live numbers but not a streaming platform. Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY fanned out over a thin WebSocket layer keeps it to one database and one deployable, with polling as the automatic fallback.

ezaz-dev.summary: The site you're reading. A static-first portfolio and writing log built to be extended one section at a time, with no build step that needs the network to succeed.

problem.lead: Portfolio sites rot. They get built on a framework that needs a rewrite every major version, hang off a CMS that outlives its usefulness, and pull live data at request time so a rate limit turns into a blank page.
points: Template-driven portfolios all read the same and are painful to change past the parts the template anticipated.
Fetching GitHub stats in the browser spends the visitor's own 60-requests-per-hour anonymous quota and shifts layout when it lands.
Content buried in markup means a copy edit is a component edit and a git diff nobody can read.
A dark mode bolted on afterwards means every colour is written twice.

solution.lead: Static output, content in JSON, and a build that is a pure offline transform. Every dynamic-feeling detail is resolved before deploy.
points: Copy lives in src/data/*.json, typed by src/lib/types.ts, so a typo surfaces at the import site instead of as a blank spot on the page.

GitHub numbers are fetched by a prebuild script into a committed cache — zero client JS, no layout shift, and a rate-limited API leaves the previous build's data in place instead of failing the deploy.
Theming is one set of CSS custom properties overridden under html.dark, so every Tailwind colour utility flips without a second class.
The bento grid is components in a grid, not a layout framework: sections are added by dropping a tile in and giving it a span.

notes.title: The build must not need the network
notes.body: GitHub data is refreshed by a standalone script before Astro runs. Beyond keeping the build a pure transform, it dodges a real failure: Node 24 on Windows aborts with a libuv assertion when Astro exits after a socket has been used, turning a green build into a non-zero exit.

notes.title: Dark mode is two load-bearing CSS rules
notes.body: The html.dark token override has to stay unlayered — Tailwind v4 emits its :root theme vars unlayered and those beat anything in @layer base — and it has to keep one real property, because Lightning CSS prunes rules that declare only custom properties and would silently drop the whole theme from production.

notes.title: Hover effects belong to the CSS, not the component
notes.body: The tile spotlight is one delegated pointermove listener in the layout writing --mx/--my. It survives view transitions without rebinding, and any page that renders a .tile gets the effect for free.

ledgerline.summary: A budgeting app that never asks for a bank login. Your ledger is a file you own, the app works offline, and sync is opt-in rather than the price of entry.

problem.lead: Budgeting tools want your bank credentials, a subscription, and permanent custody of the most sensitive data you have — and when one shuts down, the history goes with it.
points: Bank aggregation is the whole business model, so the tool needs an account, a server, and your credentials before it shows you a single number.
Exports, when they exist, are lossy CSV — the categories and rules you spent months tuning don't come with you.
The apps are useless on a plane or a bad connection, despite doing arithmetic on a few thousand rows.
Someone who just wants to know where the money went pays a monthly fee for infrastructure they never asked for.

solution.lead: Local-first by construction: the browser holds the working copy, a plain-text ledger file is the durable format, and the server is an optional relay that only ever sees encrypted blobs.
points: All reads and writes hit IndexedDB, so every interaction is instant and the app is fully usable offline.
The canonical format is an append-only plain-text ledger you can open in any editor, diff in git, and hand to another tool.
Category rules are deterministic functions over transactions, re-runnable at any time — recategorising is a replay, not a mass edit.
Optional sync ships client-encrypted deltas to Postgres; without the passphrase the server holds nothing readable.

notes.title: Local-first pushes the hard part to merges
notes.body: Making writes local is easy; making two devices agree is not. Modelling the ledger as an append-only event log with per-device ordering means conflicts resolve by concatenation, and the only genuinely ambiguous case — the same transaction edited twice — is surfaced to the user instead of silently picking a winner.

notes.title: The main thread only paints
notes.body: Parsing and reprojecting the ledger runs in a Web Worker with a structured-cloned result. Under 10k rows the difference is invisible; past that, keeping it off the main thread is the difference between a snappy filter and a locked-up tab.

notes.title: Encryption changes what the server may know
notes.body: Because deltas are encrypted client-side, the server can't validate, index, or migrate them. That constraint forced a versioned envelope from day one — the payload carries its own schema version so an old device's blob is still readable after the format moves on.
